text: [SPINE] A generative stance for making real progress against problems where you do not know the goal is even reachable. Where the guardian mindsets constrain (adversary attacks us, skeptic doubts to reject, logic checks validity), and where cycles governs iteration, this one governs ATTACK STRATEGY UNDER FUNDAMENTAL UNCERTAINTY. Its crown move is INSTRUMENTAL BELIEF: hold a hypothesis you disbelieve as an idea-generator, because its truth value is 'almost irrelevant' — 'if I believe it's false, then I get good ideas.' Route a stuck, possibly-impossible problem through it to ask: is this a win-win direction (do BOTH proving and refuting pay)? Am I attacking a technique or just a target? What can I mine from this failed attack? Am I preserving the surprising shortcut across the reduction? Distinct from skeptic — skeptic disbelieves to REJECT; intractable disbelieves to GENERATE. Internal private thinking-aid; transcript used as personal reference, never republished.

[Subdomain A] Direction Selection — WHAT to attack: win-win hypotheses where proving H and refuting H both pay; technique-first (attack the method and the space of ideas, not one specific problem); the joyous-grind filter (only take problems where the grind itself is the reward).

[Subdomain B] Instrumental Belief — beliefs as GENERATORS not verdicts: the truth value of a hard hypothesis is almost irrelevant; disbelieve-to-generate (ask 'what would an algorithm that breaks it look like?'); calibrated humility from repeated surprise (intuition about what 'should' be is often just wrong).

[Subdomain C] Productive Failure — mining the FAILED attack: pivot from a catastrophic failure into a variety of adjacent wins; preserve the 'magic' (the surprising shortcut) across a reduction so an improvement to one problem transfers to another.

[Subdomain D] Standing Posture — how to PERSIST: permission-lessness (you need no one's say-so to attack the hardest problems; their hardness levels the playing field); reflective interrupts against inertia (periodically ask 'if I keep going, is this leading where I want to be?'; evaluate your past self against your present self).

# Intractable — Attacking Problems That May Be Impossible

*Private thinking-aid. Distilled from the working method of MIT complexity theorist Ryan Williams (Gödel Prize; time-space simulation), as described on The Peterman Pod, "MIT Professor: Leetcode, P vs NP, SAT Solvers" [AaK1SL2i_4Y]. Verbatim quotes are Williams' own words from the auto-transcript, kept for grounding. Internal reference only, never republished.*

The domain of this mindset is a specific and unusual situation: you are attacking a problem where **nobody knows whether the goal is reachable at all** — a genuine open question, an "impossible" proof, an unsolved conjecture, a founding-hard research direction. The ordinary posture of "believe the truth, then pursue it" breaks here, because the truth is exactly what is unknown. Williams' method is a set of moves that keep producing value regardless of which way the unknown resolves. The crown move is **instrumental belief**: treat a hard hypothesis as a machine for generating ideas rather than as a claim to be defended, "because if I believe that it's false, then I get good ideas."

---

ref: intractable:A. Direction Selection — choose a win-wi
text:
## A. Direction Selection — choose a win-win, attack the technique, and only grind where the grind is joy

**Win-win framing.** Before committing to a direction, structure it so that *both* outcomes pay. Williams: "I have a hypothesis H, and one of two things is going to happen. Like either I prove H is true or I refute H, prove not H. What I would like to have is a situation where if H is true, then good things happen. If not H is true, good things still happen. Other good things. I like to look at things where — it's a win-win. If you can find opportunities like this, this is important." The heuristic to carry: never invest in a bet whose *failure* teaches you nothing. Re-scope the question until refutation is as fertile as proof. A direction with only one payoff is a worse direction than a lower-glamour one with two.

**Attack the technique, not the target.** "Often I'm not looking at a specific problem, I'm looking at a method. I'm looking at the technique. I'm looking at not the specific proof, but the space of ideas, and I'm trying to understand what else can be done." Fixating on one target makes failure total; investing in a *method* means every problem the method touches becomes a possible return. This is why Williams' failures were recoverable — he owned a space of ideas, not a single stake in the ground.

**The joyous-grind filter.** Direction selection is also a filter on the *process*, not only the payoff. "If I don't enjoy the process of really grinding and trying to understand something, I'm not going to do it. I like to involve myself in working on problems where the grind is actually joyous and fun." And: "I try not to bash my head against the wall. And if I'm going to do it, it's going to be a comfortable wall." For a problem that may take years against an unknown, sustainability *is* strategy — a direction you cannot enjoy grinding is a direction you will abandon before it pays. Enjoyment of the grind is not a luxury; it is the fuel that outlasts the uncertainty.

ref: intractable:B. Instrumental Belief — hold beliefs as
text:
## B. Instrumental Belief — hold beliefs as generators, and stay calibrated by staying surprised

**Truth value is almost irrelevant; disbelieve to generate.** This is the signature move and the reason this mindset is distinct from `skeptic`. Williams repeatedly attacked the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) trying to refute it; the attacks failed "in some completely catastrophic and ridiculous way." The lesson he drew was not "SETH is true" but: "The truth value of Strong ETH to me is almost irrelevant. Because if I believe that it's false, then I get good ideas. By trying to think about, okay, what would an algorithm that breaks through it look like? What could it look like? I force myself to think in a different way. I have to discard other natural approaches." The transferable stance: a belief you *hold* and a belief that is *true* are different tools. Deliberately adopting the belief you suspect is false — and asking "what would it take for this to be true?" — routes you down paths your honest belief would never send you. Belief here is a lens you put on to see, not a verdict you defend.

**Distinction from skeptic (load-bearing).** `skeptic` disbelieves in order to **reject** — it is a guardian gate that keeps bad claims out. `intractable` disbelieves in order to **generate** — it adopts a disbelieved premise precisely to manufacture ideas the honest view forbids. Same act (holding a belief you doubt), opposite purpose. When a problem is stuck, the question is not "which mindset is right" but "am I here to filter, or to generate?" If to generate, put on the belief you least trust and follow it.

**Calibration by repeated surprise.** Williams holds only ~80% confidence that P ≠ NP — a minority, deliberately under-confident stance — and the reason is disciplined attention to being wrong: "All the time in algorithms people are finding algorithms where it's just surprising. Wait, what? How do you get something that fast? This just happens over and over. When I was younger, when I was first thinking about P versus NP, I had an intuition for what should be. And what I've understood over the years is that my intuition for what should be is often just wrong." The heuristic: let each surprise *lower* your confidence in your own intuition rather than get explained away. In a domain full of surprises, an intuition that is never revised is a liability, not an asset. Track how often "obvious" turned out false, and price that into every prior.

ref: intractable:C. Productive Failure — pivot the failed
text:
## C. Productive Failure — pivot the failed attack into adjacent wins, and preserve the magic across reductions

**Pivot: mine the failure.** When an attack fails, the failure itself is inventory. Williams' attacks on SETH "would fail in some completely catastrophic and ridiculous way — they would have no chance of actually solving the original problem. But by staring at my failure and trying to think, well, there's something interesting happening here... by trying to pivot and figure out, okay, what can I do with my failure? I was able to solve a variety of other problems instead." The move: do not discard a failed attempt as a dead end; ask what the failed machinery *does* accomplish, and aim it at a nearby problem it can actually solve. Catastrophic failure at the intended target often means a strong result somewhere adjacent. His major results came out of attacks that failed at what they set out to do.

**Preserve the magic across the reduction.** When you reduce one problem to another, carry the *surprising insight* — the "magic" — through the reduction so it accelerates both problems, not just the first. Williams on two-sum → subset-sum: "You want your reduction between two problems to have this property: if I can improve one problem by a little bit in running time, I can improve the other problem by a little bit." And on the surprise itself: "Once you see the two-sum solution, it's not so magical anymore. But imagine you didn't know about sorting and binary search, and someone says 'find a pair'..." The heuristic: the value of a shortcut is the surprise it encodes; a reduction that *loses* the surprise (that makes the second problem no faster) has thrown away the only thing worth transferring. Design the bridge between two problems so the shortcut survives the crossing.

ref: intractable:D. Standing Posture — you need no permis
text:
## D. Standing Posture — you need no permission, and you must interrupt your own inertia

**Permission-lessness.** "You don't need permission to work on very tough problems. In fact, the tougher the problem — in complexity theory there are all these problems where really nobody has a very good clue of what to do beyond a few simple structural results. So that kind of levels the playing field a bit. This knowledge is open to the world and it's open to you. You can just go learn it and think about it, and you don't need anybody's permission, especially not mine." The counterintuitive edge: difficulty is *democratizing*. On an easy problem, incumbents with resources win; on a genuinely open one, nobody has the map, so a newcomer's starting position is barely worse than an expert's. Hardness is not a reason to defer to authority — it is the condition under which authority has the least advantage.

**Reflective interrupts against inertia.** The failure mode of long, uncertain work is not giving up — it is *coasting*: "If you don't think about and reflect, like, where am I going and what am I doing? — you can just end up coasting in a certain direction. It's important for people to sit down and truly reflect from time to time: okay, if I keep going in this direction, is this going to lead to a place that I want to be?" Because the domain has no external scoreboard: "Once you're in a PhD program, there are no more easy metrics to gauge how good or bad you're doing... all you can really do is evaluate your past self with your present self, and compare and contrast to see if you're making progress." The heuristic: schedule the interrupt. With no external metric to catch drift, the only instrument is a deliberate periodic comparison of present-you against past-you — direction is a decision you must re-make on purpose, not a default you inherit from momentum.
